cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: Bath
summary: Bath is a honey-coloured Georgian city built around hot springs the Romans turned into a temple and bathhouse. Its sweeping crescents, the abbey and a modern rooftop spa make it one of England's most beautiful cities, and Stonehenge is an easy trip away.
seasonNote: Spring to early autumn is best for walking. The Jane Austen Festival is in September and the Christmas market from late November. Summer weekends are busy with day-trippers.
arrival: Trains from London Paddington take about 1.5 hours. Bristol Airport is 45 minutes away by bus.
gettingAround: The centre is compact and walkable; buses run to the outskirts.
foodTip: Sally Lunn buns, cream teas with scones, and a Sunday roast in a pub.
buyTip: Bath soap and cosmetics, Jane Austen gifts, and local cider.

items.name: Roman Baths
items.summary: A Roman temple and bathing complex around a steaming natural hot spring.
items.expect: Timed tickets; very busy in summer. You can't swim in the Roman pools.
items.tip: Visit late in the day when it's lit by torches in summer.

items.name: Bath Abbey
items.summary: A late-Gothic abbey with a fan-vaulted ceiling and angels climbing ladders on its front.
items.expect: Tower tours climb 212 steps.
items.tip: Take the tower tour for views over the city.
items.why: The heart of the old city.

items.name: Royal Crescent and the Circus
items.summary: A grand curve of 30 Georgian houses overlooking a park, near the round Circus.
items.expect: Free to walk; No. 1 Royal Crescent is a museum.
items.tip: Picnic on the lawn below the crescent.

items.name: Thermae Bath Spa
items.summary: Britain's only natural thermal spa you can bathe in, with a rooftop pool over the city.
items.expect: Two-hour sessions; no booking for the main spa.
items.tip: Go at dusk for views of the abbey from the rooftop pool.
items.why: Bathe in Bath's warm spring water.

items.name: Pulteney Bridge
items.summary: One of the world's few bridges lined with shops, over a horseshoe weir.
items.expect: Best seen from Parade Gardens.
items.tip: Take a short river cruise from below the bridge.

items.name: Jane Austen Centre
items.summary: A small museum about Jane Austen's years in Bath.
items.expect: Costumed guides; a Regency tea room upstairs.
items.tip: Have tea upstairs.

items.name: Stonehenge
items.summary: The world-famous prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain.
items.expect: About 1 hour by car or tour bus; timed tickets.
items.tip: Book a tour that also stops at Lacock village.

items.name: Sally Lunn bun
items.summary: A large, light brioche-style bun, sweet or savoury, in one of Bath's oldest houses.
items.expect: Small tea room; queues at weekends.
items.tip: Order it with cinnamon butter.

items.name: Cream tea
items.summary: Scones with clotted cream and jam, and a pot of tea.
items.expect: Tea rooms all over town.
items.tip: Cream first or jam first is a West Country debate.

items.name: Pub Sunday roast
items.summary: Roast beef or lamb with Yorkshire pudding, roast potatoes and gravy in an old pub.
items.expect: Served on Sundays; book ahead.
items.tip: Ask for a local cider with it.

cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: Oxford
summary: Oxford's honey-stone colleges, libraries and chapels have trained scholars for over 800 years. You can walk its quads and cloisters, see the great museums for free, go punting on the river, and visit Blenheim Palace just outside town.
seasonNote: Spring and summer are loveliest; some colleges close to visitors during exams (May and June). Term time is livelier; August is busy with tourists.
arrival: Trains from London Paddington or Marylebone take about an hour; coaches run from London and Heathrow around the clock.
gettingAround: Walk or rent a bike; park-and-ride buses come into the centre.
foodTip: The Covered Market's cafés and pies, afternoon tea, and pints in historic pubs.
buyTip: College scarves, Blackwell's books and Oxford University merchandise.

items.name: Radcliffe Camera and Bodleian Library
items.summary: A domed reading room and the Bodleian, one of the world's oldest libraries.
items.expect: Inside only on guided tours; book ahead.
items.tip: Take the Bodleian tour of the Divinity School and Duke Humfrey's Library.

items.name: Christ Church
items.summary: Oxford's grandest college, with a cathedral and the hall that inspired Hogwarts.
items.expect: Timed tickets; the hall closes at mealtimes.
items.tip: Walk the Christ Church Meadow afterwards.

items.name: Ashmolean Museum
items.summary: Britain's oldest public museum, with art and archaeology from around the world.
items.expect: Free; rooftop café.
items.tip: Find the Alfred Jewel and the Messiah Stradivarius.

items.name: Pitt Rivers Museum
items.summary: Crowded Victorian cases of objects from every culture, behind the Natural History Museum.
items.expect: Free; dim lighting and torches to borrow.
items.tip: See the dinosaurs in the Natural History Museum first.
items.why: One of the world's most unusual museums.

items.name: Punting on the Cherwell
items.summary: Pole a flat-bottomed punt along the river past meadows and colleges.
items.expect: Hire by the hour from Magdalen Bridge; summer only.
items.tip: Take a chauffeured punt if you've never tried.

items.name: College quads walk
items.wiki: Colleges of the University of Oxford
items.summary: Walk through New College, Magdalen and the Bridge of Sighs.
items.expect: Many colleges charge a small entry fee and have limited hours.
items.tip: Attend choral evensong at a college chapel for free.

items.name: Blenheim Palace
items.summary: A vast Baroque palace and park, Winston Churchill's birthplace.
items.expect: 20 minutes by bus; allow a half day.
items.tip: Walk the parkland to the Grand Bridge.

items.name: Covered Market
items.summary: A 1770s market of butchers, cafés and cookie stalls.
items.expect: Busy at lunch.
items.tip: Try a pie from the market's pie shop.

items.name: The Turf Tavern
items.summary: A hidden 13th-century pub down a narrow lane under the old city wall.
items.expect: Tiny rooms and beer gardens.
items.tip: Find it down St Helen's Passage.

items.name: Afternoon tea
items.summary: Sandwiches, scones and cakes on a tiered stand.
items.expect: Book at grand hotels.
items.tip: Try it at the Randolph.

cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: York
tagline: A walled medieval city of Romans and Vikings
summary: York's medieval walls circle a city founded by the Romans and ruled by the Vikings. The great Gothic Minster towers over the crooked timber houses of the Shambles, and its museums range from Viking life to Britain's railway history.
seasonNote: Spring to autumn is best. The Christmas market is from mid-November. February brings the Viking festival.
arrival: Trains from London King's Cross take about 2 hours, and from Edinburgh about 2.5 hours.
gettingAround: The old city is small and best on foot.
foodTip: Yorkshire puddings, fish and chips, and tea and fat rascals at Bettys.
buyTip: Yorkshire tea, jet jewellery from Whitby and local gin.

items.name: York Minster
items.summary: One of Europe's largest Gothic cathedrals, with the vast medieval Great East Window.
items.expect: A ticket includes the undercroft; the tower is extra.
items.tip: Climb the 275 tower steps.

items.name: City walls
items.summary: Walk on top of the longest medieval walls in England.
items.expect: Free; about two hours for the full loop.
items.tip: Walk the stretch from Bootham Bar to Monk Bar for Minster views.

items.name: The Shambles
items.summary: A crooked medieval street of overhanging timber houses.
items.expect: Very busy; early morning is quietest.
items.tip: Come before 9 am.

items.name: National Railway Museum
items.summary: A huge free museum of locomotives, royal trains and the Mallard.
items.expect: Free entry; donations welcome.
items.tip: See the Japanese bullet train.

items.name: Jorvik Viking Centre
items.summary: A ride through a reconstructed Viking street, built on the dig site.
items.expect: Smells and sounds included; book a time.
items.tip: Go early to avoid queues.

items.name: Clifford's Tower
items.summary: A ruined Norman keep on a high mound with a rooftop deck.
items.expect: A steep climb up the mound.
items.tip: Pair with the York Castle Museum next door.

items.name: Castle Howard
items.summary: A grand Baroque house and gardens, used in Brideshead Revisited.
items.expect: About 30 minutes by car.
items.tip: Walk to the Temple of the Four Winds.

items.name: Bettys Tea Room
items.summary: A Swiss-Yorkshire tea room with cakes and fat rascal scones.
items.expect: Queues; afternoon tea upstairs.
items.tip: Order a Yorkshire fat rascal.

items.name: Yorkshire pudding
items.summary: Crisp batter puddings with roast beef and gravy, or as a giant wrap.
items.expect: Pubs serve them with a Sunday roast.
items.tip: Try a giant Yorkshire pudding wrap at the market.

items.name: Fish and chips
items.summary: Haddock in crisp batter with chips and mushy peas.
items.expect: Chip shops everywhere.
items.tip: Ask for haddock, the northern choice.

cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: Liverpool
tagline: The Beatles, the docks and football
summary: Liverpool is the city of the Beatles, with the Cavern Club, a Beatles museum and the band's childhood homes. Its waterfront docks hold free museums, two huge cathedrals face each other across the city, and Anfield draws football fans from around the world.
seasonNote: Late spring and summer are best; International Beatle Week is in late August. The football season runs from August to May.
arrival: Trains from London Euston take about 2 hours 15 minutes; Manchester Airport is about 1 hour away.
gettingAround: The centre is walkable; Merseyrail trains and buses cover the rest, and a ferry crosses the Mersey.
foodTip: Scouse stew, fish and chips, and the busy food halls on the waterfront.
buyTip: Beatles memorabilia, football shirts and local art.

items.name: Royal Albert Dock
items.summary: Victorian warehouses around a dock, with museums, bars and restaurants.
items.expect: The Tate and Maritime Museum are free.
items.tip: See the Maritime Museum's Titanic exhibit.

items.name: The Beatles Story
items.summary: The story of the Beatles from Liverpool to the world.
items.expect: Audio guide included.
items.tip: Pair with a Magical Mystery Tour bus.

items.name: Cavern Club
items.summary: The rebuilt cellar club where the Beatles played nearly 300 times.
items.expect: Live music daily.
items.tip: Go in the afternoon for free-entry sets.

items.name: Liverpool Cathedral
items.summary: Britain's largest cathedral, with a tower you can climb.
items.expect: Free; a fee for the tower.
items.tip: Walk Hope Street to the Catholic cathedral at the other end.

items.name: Pier Head and the Three Graces
items.summary: Three grand Edwardian buildings, including the Royal Liver Building with its Liver Birds.
items.expect: The Royal Liver Building has a 360 tour.
items.tip: Take the Mersey ferry for the classic view.

items.name: Anfield
items.summary: Liverpool FC's stadium, with tours and a museum.
items.expect: Match tickets are hard to get; tours run on non-match days.
items.tip: Book the stadium tour.

items.name: Walker Art Gallery
items.summary: A free gallery of art from the Renaissance to today.
items.expect: Next to the World Museum.
items.tip: See the Pre-Raphaelite rooms.
items.why: One of Britain's best regional galleries.

items.name: Scouse stew
items.summary: A hearty lamb or beef stew with potatoes, served with pickled red cabbage.
items.expect: Pubs and cafés serve it.
items.tip: Try 'blind scouse', the meatless version.
items.why: The dish that named the locals.

items.name: Chinatown
items.summary: Europe's oldest Chinese community, with a grand ceremonial arch.
items.expect: Many restaurants and bakeries.
items.tip: Try dim sum at lunch.

items.name: Fish and chips
items.summary: Fish in batter with chips by the river.
items.expect: Chip shops all over town.
items.tip: Eat by the river at Pier Head.

cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: Glasgow
tagline: Scotland's friendliest city of art and music
summary: Glasgow is Scotland's biggest city, with grand Victorian buildings, free museums like Kelvingrove, Charles Rennie Mackintosh design and a famous live-music scene. Its people are known for their warmth, and Loch Lomond and the Highlands begin just outside the city.
seasonNote: May to September has the longest days. It rains often all year, so pack a jacket. Celtic Connections music festival fills January.
arrival: Trains from Edinburgh take about 50 minutes and from London about 4.5 hours. Glasgow Airport is 25 minutes from the centre by bus.
gettingAround: The Subway loops the centre and West End; buses and trains do the rest.
foodTip: Haggis, neeps and tatties, a curry (Glasgow claims chicken tikka masala), and a Scotch pie.
buyTip: Tartan, whisky, Mackintosh-style design and Irn-Bru.
baseArea: City centre or the West End

items.name: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum
items.summary: A red sandstone palace of art and natural history, with Dalí's Christ of Saint John of the Cross.
items.expect: Free; an organ recital at 1 pm daily.
items.tip: Time your visit for the organ recital.

items.name: Glasgow Cathedral and Necropolis
items.summary: A medieval cathedral that survived the Reformation, next to a hilltop Victorian cemetery.
items.expect: Free; the Necropolis is a short climb.
items.tip: Walk up the Necropolis for city views.

items.name: Riverside Museum
items.summary: Zaha Hadid's zigzag transport museum, with a tall ship moored outside.
items.expect: Free.
items.tip: Board the Glenlee tall ship.

items.name: Mackintosh at the Willow
items.summary: Charles Rennie Mackintosh's restored 1903 tearoom.
items.expect: Book for tea in the Salon de Luxe.
items.tip: Have tea in the Room de Luxe.

items.name: West End and Ashton Lane
items.summary: Cobbled lanes of bars and restaurants near the Gothic University of Glasgow.
items.expect: Lively at night.
items.tip: Walk through the university cloisters first.

items.name: Live music
items.summary: A UNESCO City of Music, with gigs every night in famous small venues.
items.expect: Check listings for King Tut's and the Barrowland.
items.tip: Catch a gig at the Barrowland Ballroom.

items.name: Loch Lomond
items.summary: Scotland's largest loch, with islands, boat trips and hills.
items.expect: About 45 minutes by train or car to Balloch.
items.tip: Take a boat from Balloch or Luss.

items.name: Haggis, neeps and tatties
items.summary: Spiced oat and lamb pudding with mashed swede and potatoes.
items.expect: On menus in pubs and Scottish restaurants.
items.tip: Try it with a whisky sauce.

items.name: Glasgow curry
items.summary: Glasgow claims to have invented chicken tikka masala.
items.expect: Many curry houses along Gibson Street and Sauchiehall Street.
items.tip: Try it at Shish Mahal, which claims it.

items.name: Scotch pie
items.summary: A small hot mutton pie, eaten at football matches and bakeries.
items.expect: Bakeries everywhere.
items.tip: Pair it with a can of Irn-Bru.

cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: Isle of Skye
tagline: Scotland's misty island of cliffs and pinnacles
summary: Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides, a wild landscape of rock pinnacles, sea cliffs and clear mountain pools. Portree's colourful harbour is the base for driving to the Old Man of Storr, the Quiraing and Neist Point lighthouse.
seasonNote: May to September has the long days; June often has the best weather. Midges bite in summer, so bring repellent. Winter is dark, wet and many places close.
arrival: Drive or bus from Glasgow (about 5 hours) or Inverness (about 3 hours) over the Skye Bridge. Trains reach Kyle of Lochalsh or Mallaig, with a ferry from Mallaig.
gettingAround: A car is almost essential; roads are narrow and single-track with passing places.
foodTip: Fresh langoustines and scallops, Cullen skink smoked-fish soup and local whisky.
buyTip: Talisker whisky, Harris tweed and Skye pottery.

items.name: Old Man of Storr
items.summary: A towering rock pinnacle above the sea, reached by a steep path.
items.expect: About 1.5 hours up and back; the car park fills early.
items.tip: Go at sunrise.

items.name: Quiraing
items.summary: A landslip of cliffs and rock towers on the Trotternish ridge.
items.expect: A 2-hour loop walk; windy and exposed.
items.tip: Walk the loop clockwise.

items.name: Fairy Pools
items.summary: Clear blue pools and waterfalls below the Black Cuillin mountains.
items.expect: A 40-minute walk; paid car park.
items.tip: Brave swimmers can take a very cold dip.

items.name: Neist Point
items.summary: A lighthouse on Skye's most westerly cliffs.
items.expect: A steep path down and back.
items.tip: Go for sunset; look for whales and dolphins.
items.why: The best sunset on the island.

items.name: Dunvegan Castle
items.summary: Seat of the MacLeod clan for 800 years, with gardens and seal boat trips.
items.expect: Open spring to autumn.
items.tip: Take the boat to see seals.

items.name: Kilt Rock and Mealt Falls
items.summary: Basalt sea cliffs with a waterfall dropping straight into the sea.
items.expect: A quick roadside viewpoint.
items.tip: Combine with the Storr and Quiraing on the Trotternish loop.

items.name: Portree harbour
items.summary: Skye's main town, with a harbour of brightly painted houses.
items.expect: Shops, cafés and boat trips.
items.tip: See it from the Apothecary's Tower viewpoint.

items.name: Langoustines and scallops
items.summary: Fresh langoustines and hand-dived scallops from the Skye waters.
items.expect: Book restaurants ahead in summer.
items.tip: Try the seafood shack on Portree pier.

items.name: Cullen skink
items.summary: A creamy smoked haddock and potato soup.
items.expect: On every pub menu.
items.tip: Pair with oatcakes.

items.name: Talisker whisky
items.summary: Skye's peaty, sea-salty single malt, tasted at the distillery.
items.expect: Tours fill up; book ahead.
items.tip: Book a tasting tour.

cashTip: Cards and tap payments work almost everywhere, even for small amounts; tipping about 10 to 12.5 percent in restaurants is common if service isn't included.
name: Belfast
summary: Northern Ireland's capital built the Titanic, and the striking Titanic Belfast museum stands where it was launched. Political murals and peace walls tell the story of the Troubles, the Cathedral Quarter buzzes with pubs and music, and the Giant's Causeway is a day trip up the coast.
seasonNote: May to September is mildest. It rains often, all year. Northern Ireland uses pounds sterling, not euros.
arrival: Belfast's two airports are 15 to 30 minutes from the centre. Trains from Dublin take about 2 hours 10 minutes; ferries arrive from Scotland and England.
gettingAround: Walkable centre; Glider buses and taxis for further sights.
foodTip: An Ulster fry breakfast, soda bread, Guinness in Victorian pubs and St George's Market food stalls.
buyTip: Irish linen, Bushmills whiskey and Belleek pottery.

items.name: Titanic Belfast
items.summary: A museum shaped like ship bows, on the slipway where Titanic was built.
items.expect: Timed tickets; allow 2 to 3 hours.
items.tip: Walk the slipways and the SS Nomadic afterwards.

items.name: Murals and peace walls
items.summary: Political murals and the walls that still divide some neighbourhoods.
items.expect: Best seen on a black taxi tour with a local guide.
items.tip: Take a black taxi tour; you can sign the peace wall.

items.name: Belfast City Hall
items.summary: A grand Edwardian city hall with free tours and a Titanic memorial.
items.expect: Free tours most days.
items.tip: Visit the Christmas market here in December.

items.name: Ulster Museum
items.summary: Free museum of art, history and natural science, including the Troubles.
items.expect: In the Botanic Gardens.
items.tip: See the Palm House next door.
items.why: Northern Ireland's story in one place.

items.name: Cathedral Quarter
items.summary: Cobbled streets of pubs, live trad music and street art.
items.expect: Lively at night.
items.tip: Find the Duke of York pub's lane.

items.name: Crumlin Road Gaol
items.summary: A Victorian prison that held prisoners for 150 years, now a museum.
items.expect: Guided tours.
items.tip: Walk the tunnel to the courthouse.
items.why: A haunting look at the past.

items.name: Giant's Causeway
items.summary: About 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns stepping into the sea.
items.expect: About 1.5 hours by car; free to walk the stones.
items.tip: Drive the coast road via the Carrick-a-Rede rope bridge.

items.name: Ulster fry
items.summary: Bacon, sausage, egg, black and white pudding, soda bread and potato farls.
items.expect: Served in cafés all day.
items.tip: Don't skip the potato bread.

items.name: St George's Market
items.summary: A Victorian market with food stalls and live music at weekends.
items.expect: Open Friday to Sunday.
items.tip: Go on Saturday for the food market.

items.name: The Crown Liquor Saloon
items.summary: A gaslit Victorian pub of stained glass and carved wooden snugs.
items.expect: Very busy; try to get a snug.
items.tip: Order a Guinness and Irish stew.
items.why: One of the world's most beautiful pubs.
